content.text: assumed audience

I wrote this with the perspective of my past self in mind. You may be different from me, and so you may not find all the sections in this post helpful. Here's a brief list of the target audience of this post:
You're interested in applying to the US for a four-year bachelor's degree
You're aiming for top schools
You're applying through the CommonApp
This is the main application pathway. There are alternatives (mainly the Coalition App), but those generally support a smaller number of colleges.
If you're in a US high school, QuestBridge could also be of interest to you.
terminology
college = university = school
T20 = Top 20 (schools), according to the US News rankings
money

Before all else, let's figure out if it's financially feasible for you to attend college in the US. The college application process is long, and I wouldn't embark on it until you have a plan for how to afford it.
If money isn't an issue, feel free to skip this section!
it costs $400K total, before aid/scholarships

Most top American private universities cost roughly $100K USD a year for four years, so that evens out to $400K USD total. The good news is that this total includes everything (cost of tuition, housing, food, travel costs, books, etc.). The bad news is, well, it's really expensive.
Again, if this amount is not a problem for you, skip this section :)
Fortunately, there's three main options that can help with that. I'll go through them in order of best to worst (in my opinion):
Financial aid (need-based)
Scholarships (merit)
Loans
Quick note: the following mainly applies to selective,
private
schools in the US. These schools are generally really rich, liberal, and ridiculously hard to get into.
financial aid

Here's how financial aid works: the university looks at how much money your household makes and compares that against the $400K price tag from earlier. If you have very little money, it'll waive all fees and let you attend for free. Sometimes it might even pay you to attend. If you have some money, it may slash your cost down to a few thousand dollars a year.

This all sounds amazing. The catch? Generous financial-aid policies are generally only offered by the most selective schools in the US, and only the private ones -- basically, the Harvards, Princetons, and Yales of the world. You're guaranteed to be able to afford it, but only IF you can get in in the first place. The other catch is that there are sometimes people who fall into a bracket where their families make too much money for them to receive substantial amounts of financial aid, but not enough for them to actually afford the cost of attendance.

If you're unsure about how much aid you'd qualify for, check! Most universities have a financial aid calculator that will give you an estimate of how much aid you'd qualify for based on your household income. Just search for "[insert university name] financial aid calculator" in your browser.

In order to get financial aid, you'll have to explicitly apply for it when you apply to colleges (via the CSS Profile). Colleges can see that you are requesting financial aid, and they will (usually) take that into consideration when deciding whether or not to admit you. This means that applying for financial aid can and will decrease your chances of admission.
need-blind vs need-aware
You might see these terms come up on a college's website. Here's what they mean:
Need-blind: Applying for financial aid WILL NOT affect your chances of admission
Need-aware: Applying for financial aid WILL affect your chances of admission
Most US schools are need-blind for
domestic
applicants, which refers to US citizens or permanent residents. As of May 2026, these are the schools that are need-blind for
international students
Amherst College
Bowdoin College
Brown University
Dartmouth College
Harvard University
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Princeton University
University of Notre Dame
Washington and Lee University
Yale University

You may sometimes see a school declare that it is need-blind, but unless it explicitly says that that policy also applies to international students, you can assume it is need-aware instead. This doesn't mean you can't get into a school that is not need-blind, just that it will affect your chances of getting in, and I think you should know that upfront.
"fulfils 100% demonstrated need"

This means that if the school has decided that you'll need $60K a year of financial aid to attend, and they admit you, they will give you the full $60K a year. Most top schools do this, and you should look out for this statement when applying. Otherwise you may get into a situation where the school knows you need $60K, but they only give you $30K.
scholarships

Scholarships are usually merit-based. This means that scholarship applications usually consider your grades, achievements (e.g. winning competitions), academic/research publications, community impact (e.g. if you have a company/non-profit that helped X number of people), or, more broadly, something that you've done. This is different from financial aid, because financial aid is granted based on your family's financial situation.

Scholarships are pretty limited in US universities. If you go down the college application rabbit hole, you may encounter some seemingly big scholarships like Coca-Cola, but these are usually limited to US citizens/permanent residents, which you don't qualify for as an international student.

However, a handful of US universities do offer scholarships to their students. Some of these scholarships require separate applications, and some don't (meaning you are immediately considered for the scholarship if you apply to the college).
I am a receipient of one of these scholarships, the Cornelius Vanderbilt Scholarship, which covers the cost of tuition for four years.

Scholarships and financial aid are not mutually exclusive, you can receive both at the same time. For example, my scholarship covers the cost of tuition, but I receive additional financial aid on top of that that helps me pay for housing and food.
the catch
Not many universities offer scholarships. This is an extremely incomplete list, of course, but here are the ones I know of:
Vanderbilt University (separate application for each scholarship, deadline: Dec 1)
Cornelius Vanderbilt: full-tuition
Ingram: full-tuition + housing
Chancellor's: full-tuition
Technically you can be considered for this without applying but I'd suggest you just apply if you're interested. There's too many students and too little scholarships to go around.
Duke University*
Alumni Endowed Scholarship
Angier B. Duke Scholarship
Benjamin N. Duke Scholarship
Karsh International Scholarship
Trinity Scholarships
University Scholarship
Robertson Scholars Program (the only one that requires a separate application)
*some of these may not accept international students, sorry I haven't looked through them too thoroughly!
loans

I'm very anti-loan, because I didn't want the burden of student loans over my head as I was studying/working. If you're interested in taking out loans, you might want to consider what repayment will look like. How much will you need to pay every month, and for how long?

Keep in mind that "prospective [international] students must have the financial resources to live and study in the United States. This includes being able to cover the cost of tuition, books, living expenses and travel. Prospective students must bring their evidence of financial ability when applying for their student visa with the U.S. Department of State”, according to the US government.

This is not legal financial advice, but before taking out a loan, I'd encourage you to analyze how much your loan amount is in comparison to the cost of attendance of your uni. Even if you think it's worth the loan, your visa might not be accepted if you lack the ability to pay.

That said, loans are a path taken by a lot of American students to pay for college. Unfortunately I don't know what reputable loan options are available for international students. I believe most US-based loans will require someone living in the US to act as a guarantor for you.
one more thing

You must pay to submit an application to each school. This application fee is roughly ~$80 USD per school. Thankfully, the fee can be waived for most schools if you get a letter from your principal/program coordinator/whoever is in charge of whatever it is you're studying. The letter needs to talk about why the fee would be expensive for you, so something like:
You have a bunch of siblings who all have education costs
A family member needs expensive medical treatment
I had all my fees waived except for Rice, which doesn't allow this.
the US education system
Okay, we figured out the money problem, so it's crash course time! Here's a list of things you should know:
Bachelor's degrees typically take 4 years (not 3 like the UK)
The academic year typically starts in August or September and runs until May or June. You generally have about 3 1/2 months of summer break in between each year
A map of the years to what people call them:
1st year
Freshman
2nd year
Sophomore
3rd year
Junior
4th year
Senior

For most universities (that I applied to), you apply to the university itself, not to the major that you chose. So if you're applying to Vanderbilt University for Computer Science, the Vanderbilt part matters a lot more than the computer science part.
This is because it is generally easy to change your major once you've gotten into the school. For example, I applied as a physics major, and now I'm a computer science major.

Why is this relevant? Because sometimes it's easier to get into some schools if you apply as a certain major. For example, a lot of people apply to Stanford for computer science, so you might have a better chance of getting in if you apply as a classics major instead.

A possible exception: if switching majors also requires switching between "schools" within a university (e.g., from the Arts and Science school to the Engineering school), it might be more difficult at certain universities. Check with the schools that you're interested in.
Double majoring is a relatively common thing to do in most schools (But not all! Princeton did not allow double majoring until pretty recently. Check with the school that you're interested in).
This means that in general, it's not uncommon for people to graduate with a bachelor's in physics and math, computer science and math, english and classics, etc.
Sometimes people even triple major! This is pretty uncommon though.
Schools either have three semesters (fall, spring, summer), or four semesters (add winter). You have breaks between semesters and sometimes during semesters, but there are not many of them.
applying, step 0: high school grades

The application will ask for four years of your academic results (translated) in English, a list of your achievements, and a list of your leadership roles. This means that you need to have been a great student for a few years before applying. Yes, this is brutal, but that's what the application wants.

Each of these four years should also consist of (at least) two sets of grades, like a midterm and a final, or trials and actual exam grades. I got away with one set of grades for the 2020 school year because of COVID, but I don't know how strict they are with this nowadays. It's probably better to send as many grades as you can
translating grades

You can do this yourself, it doesn't have to be anything too special. I did mine in Google Sheets and it was fine. Try to match the formats, if there are tables in the original transcript, make tables in your translated transcript. Match the formatting and spacing if you can. That helps it look a little more legitimate.
some tips for A Level takers

If you're doing the A Levels program like I was, you can use your AS and A Levels as two separate years, regardless of when you took each exam. So your 4 years of grades will look something like this:
Second last year of high/secondary school (midterms and finals)
Last year of high/secondary school (midterms and finals)
AS Levels (trials and actual)
A Levels (trials and actual)
This can help you if you got better grades in the A Level program than in high/secondary school. If you're in the opposite situation, you can do this instead:
Third-last year of high/secondary school (midterms and finals)
Second-last year of high/secondary school (midterms and finals)
Last year of high/secondary school (midterms and finals)
AS & A Levels (only actual grades)

If your grades haven't come out by the application deadline, you can and should use your forecasted/trial grades. Which does mean that yes, your chances of admission lean pretty heavily on how nice your lecturers are. You might want to suck up to them a little (I'm only slightly kidding).
applying, step 1: essays
the CommonApp essay
Most students apply through the CommonApp. The biggest thing you'll hear when talking about the CommonApp is the CommonApp essay. Details:
250 - 650 words
You should be right around that 630-650 word range though, to maximize your chances!
Prompts, choose one (2025-26 application cycle):

Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.

The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?
Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea. What prompted your thinking? What was the outcome?
Reflect on something that someone has done for you that has made you happy or thankful in a surprising way. How has this gratitude affected or motivated you?
Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.
Describe a topic, idea, or concept you find so engaging that it makes you lose all track of time. Why does it captivate you? What or who do you turn to when you want to learn more?
Share an essay on any topic of your choice. It can be one you've already written, one that responds to a different prompt, or one of your own design.

Very important: This essay is meant to be quirky, unstructured, unique, etc. You SHOULD NOT write a generic starting line like "My name is [...] and I'm interested in [major] because [reason]". The CommonApp essay is NOT like the UCAS Personal Statement for the UK. You are NOT meant to repeat your academic achievements or explain why you're qualified for the schools that you're applying to. Instead, the CommonApp essay is meant to be a story about your life.

Think a super-mini autobiography. It should read like one cohesive narrative, so all the paragraphs should come together to talk about one thing instead of each paragraph focusing on a different aspect of you. It's more story-writing than essay-writing, honestly.
If you're confused, try reading some of the Harvard-accepted essays for inspiration.
college-specific essays
Most colleges are going to have specific essay requirements. I'm not going to go into depth because they're all sort of different but here's some examples:
The intellectual vitality essay (essentially: what are you curious about and why?)
The roommate essay (write to your future roommate)
The "Why This School?" essay
The "Why This Major?" essay
Like I mentioned, you don't need to select a major when applying, and if you do select one, you're not bound to that major.

If you don't select a major, usually these types of essays will just turn into an exploration about a few fields that you're curious about, e.g. maybe you're unsure about math or physics or computer science because you're interested in all of them, so then you'd just write about what it is that you're interested in.
applying, step 2: honors and activities
Honors: stuff you've won. Activities: stuff you've done. Make a list of these, and try to order them roughly in terms of how many years you've done them for or how impressive they are.
The CommonApp lets you list 10 activities and 5 honors. If you can, fill them all, but don't make stuff up for the sake of it. It's fine to leave one or two spots blank.
applying, step 3: letters of recommendation(s)

You'll need to pick a person to write you a letter that talks about how great you are. Usually, different colleges will have different requirements for who this person can be. Here's a list of people you can ask, roughly ordered from most ideal to least ideal:
Professor/lecturer (college or university level)
Teacher (high school level)
Sports coach/piano teacher/etc
Family member/friend

The letter has to be in English, but I believe they can be translated if they need to be. How this generally works is you'll invite the person via email to make an account on the CommonApp platform, and they'll submit their application via their account. The idea is that you shouldn't be able to see your own letters. However depending on who you ask and their familiarity with English and how much they like you, you might be able to write your own letters and submit them via their email. I totally would never do that.
Some good things for the letter:
Written by someone who has watched you grow in some sense,
e.g. a piano teacher who taught you for many years, or a teacher who watched you improve from a C to an A.
applying, step 4: tests
standardized tests: SAT/ACT
I only took the SAT because the ACT had a science component and I didn't want to take a science test. I am therefore unqualified to talk about the ACT, sorry. But here's a brief breakdown of the SAT:
Two sections, English and Maths
All objective/multiple-choice questions
Generally meant to be taken by 15-17 year olds
English:
Read a passage, then answer questions about it
Figure out what the author would think about [some topic] based on the passage
The level of English was much harder than what I was anticipating
Maths:
Algebra, basic calculus (differentiation & integration), trigonometry, etc.
I found this pretty equivalent to my year 10/11 maths syllabus, it wasn't too hard

A bunch of schools went test-optional during COVID, meaning they did not require applicants to submit SAT/ACT scores. Some of these schools are now rolling back that policy and mandating test scores. In general, if you're good at test-taking, I strongly recommend you take one of these tests and submit the scores to colleges. A good score can only help your application.
You can take these tests multiple times to improve your score.
TOEFL/IELTS/Duolingo English Test

These tests check your proficiency in English. They are roughly equivalent in difficulty and most schools will accept both the TOEFL and IELTS without a strong preference. The Duolingo test is not as widely accepted. TOEFL might be the slightly better option just because it was designed for the US (IELTS was designed for the UK), but any of these tests are fine as long as they're accepted by the schools you're applying to.
Some international students will be required to take one of these tests. Here's the rough list of things that would exempt you from this requirement:
You've attended an international school/school where the primary language is English for at least ~4 years.
English is your native language
The list might be different at different schools, so check with each school that you're applying to.
comparing schools
To be honest, I never really compared schools while applying because all I wanted was to get into
a
T20 school in the US. I really didn't care which one it was. And then I only got accepted into one school, so...

I have, however, realized through my time at Vanderbilt that I got extremely lucky with Vanderbilt. I've realized that I would have had a miserable time at some of my "dream" schools (Princeton and Cornell).
touring the campuses
This is the most expensive and time-intensive option, but it's the best if it works for you geographically/financially.

You can typically book guided tours of a university during the academic year, where a student will show you around and tell you a little bit of propaganda about their school. Most campus grounds are also open to the public to wander around in (which is why you'll always see tourists taking pictures at Harvard), so you could also just walk in and gauge how big the campus is, how far the dorms are to the classrooms, talk to some students about the quality of the classes/alumni network/clubs, etc.

If you're comparing a bunch of schools that accepted you in order to pick one to attend, most schools will invite admitted students to tour their campus and show off some of their facilities/staff/offerings to try to get you to accept their offer.
locations

There are colleges located in the busiest of cities (e.g. Columbia/NYU in New York City), in slightly quieter cities (e.g. Harvard/MIT/the dozen other colleges in Boston/Cambridge), in an alcove slightly away from their city (e.g. Vanderbilt in Nashville), and in the middle of nowhere (e.g. Dartmouth and Cornell).

The weather is also drastically different between Texas/Arizona and New York/Massachusetts. If you're coming from an extremely hot country, maybe consider whether or not you can actually survive in upstate New York where it's below or close to freezing for about six months.
grade deflation vs grade inflation

Some universities like Princeton and UPenn are known for really bad grade deflation, meaning that they will push the average grade in a class down if it's too high. I don't know what this means exactly in practice, but it usually means that only a few people in a class can get As, no matter how smart everyone in the class actually is.

On the other hand, some colleges like Harvard have pretty notorious grade inflation. I think Harvard actually had to implement stricter rules for their latin honors because about 70% of students were graduating with honors.
city campus or college campus

Somewhat related to the previous point. Some universities have a dedicated plot of land where all/most of their buildings are located. Vanderbilt is like this. Some other universities have a bunch of buildings scattered throughout the city that they're located in. NYU is like that.

You may prefer one over the other. I really like having a short commute from my bed to my class. I like the college campus vibe, and that means I like having a place to hang out on campus that is separate from the non-campus outside. I also don't really like going out to the city during weekends, so I don't mind the fact that the city is further away. In fact, I kind of like it, because I get to stay away from the ruckus of the party scene unless I specifically want to try it out on a certain day.

title: everything you need to know about applying to US unis as an int'l student
